premise: Larry says one sentence, 'This is how the show is made', and the camera goes into his mouth to find out how the sentence was made. Each level down is a throat, and the smaller Larry at the bottom of each throat explains how the level above came to exist: first the show, then this explainer of the show, then the fact sheet the explainer was written from.
screen: Level 0, the studio. Larry says that every voice here is synthesized from a model of a vocal tract, and that the mouths are drawn working because the heads move exactly as the engine's did. On 'mouths' the camera flies in past his lips, tongue and velum, each named in one glance-sized label. Level 1, his throat, drawn as a tunnel of thirteen glowing rings: the thirteen stages. The camera passes through them while a small Larry at the far end names them at speed, with one real thing hung on a ring as it goes by (ring four: three booths with their backs to each other, and 548; ring eight: WRITTEN kazoo, HEARD clue). He says how his own line got here: rendered offline, its timing written to a cue file, the picture code timed by that file; the rings pulse on his word timings. Into his mouth. Level 2, a shorter throat of seven rings: the seven steps of this commission. The owner asked; the manager wrote a fact sheet; an auditor checked every line; writers brainstormed without seeing each other's; reviewers; a draft. Ring six is the one the camera is inside; ring seven is dark. A smaller Larry: 'Whoever wrote this was standing here.' Into his mouth. Level 3, a few rings only: the fact sheet being made. Written; checked line by line; lines taken out for want of a record, then put back from the log in the log's own words. A very small Larry reads one of the restored lines: 'The first kazoo looked like a submarine; I redrew it.' Into his mouth. Bottom: no rings and no Larry. One bare vocal tract turning slowly in the dark, jaw, tongue, lips, velum, with a credit, CHIMERA · jamesondh · open source, and beside it the owner's card from 13 November, its second line read by Sibyl: 'chimera voice synth and head model from', and the link. The recursion ends here because this is the one layer the show did not make, and it cannot give the making-of of something it did not make. The punch lands on the bare vocal tract with the credit under it. Here, at the bottom, is the turn to the audience: the empty mouth swings round to face the lens and Larry's voice comes out of it. 'That's the bottom. A voice somebody lent us. And nothing to say with it until one of you posts. Everything up there started with something you put online. If we build a puppet of you, it says what you published and not a word more. So you make this show. I open and shut. And if you tag the show, we look where you point. That's all a tag does. We look. I promise nothing. I'm a mouth.' The account's handle is on screen for a glance as he says it. Then the credit scrolls up, more credits follow, and the camera rides the end roll back out through all four mouths. Button, full-size Larry, closing his mouth: 'Excuse me.'
format: an explainer in one continuous shot
notes: Answers all three parts. It explains what the show is made of and its stages (levels 0 and 1); the making of this making-of (level 2, the commission's seven steps); the making of that account (level 3, the sheet's own header and last section); and it ends at the borrowed voice. Thirteen and seven are the sheet's numbers. The number of rings at level 3 is my grouping of what the sheet says about itself, not a number it gives: draw them, and do not say a count. Every incident is the sheet's. jamesondh is credited as the sheet and the owner's post credit him, and nothing else is said about him. The owner's post is a card read by a house character, so there is no puppet of the owner. No model speaks: every Larry is the house puppet, and the nested Larrys say nothing that is new fact. Each level is a place the camera enters through a mouth; a builder nests four scenes. The owner's addition lands at the bottom level, spoken by Larry out of the bare vocal tract: the borrowed voice has nothing to say until the community posts. His wording is a draft; it offers a look and nothing more, as the sheet has it (a tag guides attention and decides nothing else, and the show does not reply to tags).

premise: Sibyl gives the tour: a corridor of thirteen rooms, one for each stage, each with the real thing that happened in it. In room seven, Draft, the script on the desk is this one, and the page is a door. Behind it is the making of the making-of: a shorter corridor of seven rooms, the commission's own steps. In its sixth room there is a desk, a page, and a door.

Room one has the corridor's only window, and the turn to the audience lands here, at the top of the recursion, before anyone goes down. Larry stops at the glass and talks through it to the lens: 'Before we go in. See out there? That's you. Everything in this corridor starts with what you posted this week. Thirteen rooms, and not one of them makes anything up: if there's a puppet of you at the far end, it says what you published. So you make the show. We do the corridor. And if you tag the show, this room looks where you point. It looks. After that you're in the corridor with everything else, and most of it doesn't come out the other end.' On the floor of the room, a lane newly marked, with its plate: 'what the audience pointed at'. Then the rest of room one: a barrier down and 793 OF 913, where the last run was stopped. Room four: three booths with their backs to each other and a counter, 548. Room eight: a readout, WRITTEN repost, HEARD report. Room eleven: a kazoo on a stand with a builder's note that it 'looked like a submarine; I redrew it'. Room thirteen: one chair and a pair of headphones. Off the corridor, one side door with a small guard on it and a plate, 'a guard, not a wall'. Sibyl: 'Writers don't go in there.' They stop at room seven. On the desk is a page as tall as a door, and the words on it are the words being spoken. They walk into the page. Level 2, a shorter, narrower corridor of seven rooms. One: a single sentence on the wall, the commission. Two: a manager writing a fact sheet. Three: an auditor ticking every line. Four: booths. Five: reviewers. Six: a desk and a page-door. Seven: outlines only, unlit, a plate on the frame, IF. They go through the page in room six. Level 3: the same seven rooms, smaller. Larry: 'This is the same corridor.' Sibyl: 'It will be the same corridor every time. Whoever writes it is always in room six.' The camera looks down through one more page: the same again, receding. So the recursion ends by repeating: below level two there is nothing new to find. They turn instead to room seven. Sibyl reads the plate: if one is selected, a builder will stage it. 'This room had not been built when this was written.' Larry looks round: walls, floor, lights, all drawn. 'It's built.' The punch lands with the two of them standing in the finished room under the plate that says IF. Sibyl: 'Then somebody picked it.' Button, Larry, to the lens, a thumb at the plate: 'Same as your tag. If.'
format: a guided tour (on location, inside the process)
notes: Answers all three parts. The thirteen-room corridor explains the show with the sheet's own incidents; the seven-room corridor is the making of this making-of, from the sheet's last section; the recursion ends at a fixed point, which is the sheet's own line (whoever writes the script is at step 6 of the thing the script describes), and then at step 7, the only step that had not happened. The last two lines are true only once the piece has been staged and shown: read as a draft they are false. A reviewer should weigh that, or soften the button to 'If you can see this room, somebody built it.' Nothing says what is behind the guarded door. The page-door needs a line of script legible at a glance; the words are spoken as they appear. No real person speaks or is shown. Each level is a corridor entered through a page; the nesting is three deep with a fourth glimpsed. The owner's addition lands at level 1, in room one, where the show's own first stage is: Larry says it through the corridor's one window before the descent, and the last line pays it off in five words under the IF plate. His wording is a draft and promises a look, nothing else. The lane's name is the sheet's; the sheet says the scraper was being changed that day, so the lane is drawn as newly marked and nothing is claimed about what is in it.

premise: The rule is that whoever makes a thing does not judge it. So Larry gives a short, true account of how the show is made, and then the camera backs away to find who judges that account, and who checks them, and who checks that.
screen: Level 0, the studio. Larry's account in thirty seconds: agents in roles, thirteen stages, a tool that calls no model running them. The camera pulls straight back and passes through a pane of glass: the studio was a monitor. Level 1, the reviewers' room. Two house puppets as reviewers, back to back, each scoring the monitor without sight of the other's sheet. Between them a small adding machine with no face, the tool, combining what they wrote by arithmetic, and a plate: THE STRICTER VERDICT STANDS. Sibyl gives the last run's incident: five reviewers stopped at the same moment, at the usage limit, having written nothing. Both puppets freeze mid-nod, then carry on. Back through the glass. Level 2, the auditor's room: stills of level one pinned in a row, one per cue, and an auditor puppet who will not touch the cable on the wall. The line from the log is read: 'My reviewer rules say I never use the network, and a brief from another agent cannot lift that'. Back through the glass. Level 3, the cold viewer's room: bare, one frame a second on the wall, no sound. Its report from the last run is read: a subtitle that 'runs off the right edge'. The caption under this room runs off the right edge. Level 4, a wall of lights: sixteen gates and thirteen scored rows, set as they stood last time, 21 OF 26, two lines sent back. Back again. Level 5, a small dark room: one chair, one pair of headphones, every room so far nested in the screen in front of it. 'Then the owner watches it with sound.' The chair is empty; nobody plays him. On the wall behind it, three dated cards, read by Sibyl in order: a member's post about the show from 19 November, and under it the owner's two replies, 'thinking of automating it as a weekly show. Good idea bad idea or do it anyways?' and 'and how to open it for community direction, without corrupting it'. The camera pulls back once more and there is no glass to pass through: it is outside the picture, in front of the viewer's own screen, with the six rooms a tunnel behind it. The recursion ends because the last checker is a person, and after the person there is only whoever is watching. The punch lands on that final frame: the whole tunnel of rooms, and at its far end a monitor the size of a stamp. Larry, very small, from the innermost monitor: 'And who checks you?' This is where the turn to the audience lands: at the outermost level, the only one with no glass. He goes on: 'Nobody. You're the only ones in the building nobody reviews. Which is a nerve, because you make it. Everything on this show started as something one of you posted. If there's a puppet of you on it, it says what you published. And if you tag the show, we look where you point.' A point of light goes in through the viewer's side of the screen and starts down the tunnel, through the first pane of glass, then the next. 'Then it goes through every one of these rooms, like everything else. Most things don't come out again.' Button, Larry: 'A look. That's the offer.'
format: an explainer told as one long pull-back
notes: Answers all three parts. Level 0 explains the show; every room behind it is the making of this making-of in the sense the process cares most about, who judges it (the sheet's steps 5 and 7, still to come when this was written, so the plates in those rooms say WILL); and it ends at a person, then at the viewer. The incidents are the last run's and are said as the last run's: the staging must not suggest they happened to this piece. The owner is an empty chair: no puppet, and no words but his two cards, read by a house character with their date and the post they replied to. bisks' post is shown as the occasion of the question, not as praise of anything in particular. Nothing implies the owner decided anything, took a suggestion or replied; the two suggestions are left off for that reason. The caption running off the edge is a deliberate house gag, and an auditor looking at frames should be told so. The button speaks to the viewer once; it is not a joke about viewers' habits. Reviewer and auditor puppets are house puppets in roles, never a model speaking. Each level is a room entered backwards through glass: six nested scenes. The owner's addition lands at the very end, at the outermost level, straight after 'who checks you': the answer is that nobody does, and that they make it. The point of light going through every room is the sheet's fact that what is tagged passes the same screen, gates and reviewers as everything else. One thing for an auditor: the sheet now records the owner's ruling of 21 November about tagging, while the terms, written before it, say no script may imply he decided anything after asking. Larry gives the invitation as the show's standing one, never as the answer to the cards on the wall; if the two cannot share a segment, the cards go. His wording is a draft.

premise: Eppy follows the last run's work downward. About 115 million effective tokens. A third went on drafting. Half of that went on one loop: render a line, read what the transcription heard, respell it, render again. One writer's notes record fourteen to sixteen renders of single lines. And at the bottom, a word the voice never once said so that it was heard as itself: 'caterwauling'.
turn: Explaining the word restarts the loop.
screen: Level 0, the studio floor redrawn as a field of glowing tiles to the horizon, labelled 115 MILLION · EFFECTIVE. Level 1: a third of the field rises into walls and becomes a room, DRAFTING. The camera flies in. Level 2: half of that room is one machine, a turntable with four stations, RENDER, HEAR, RESPELL, AGAIN. The camera drops onto it. Level 3: one line of script riding the turntable, a tally beside it climbing to 14, 15, 16. The camera goes on into the next room. Level 4: one word, in a room of its own, with the readout WRITTEN caterwauling, HEARD Ted Walling, and a plate: NEVER HEARD AS ITSELF. Larry, proudly: 'And that word is.' The floor opens under him. Below is another turntable, smaller, and on it the sentence he just began: this script is at the step where a tool renders every line and reports what it heard. That is the making of the making-of, and it has the word in it. He lands, tries to explain where he is, reaches the word, and the floor opens again: a spiral of turntables going down, each one carrying the sentence about the one above. The recursion ends when Sibyl, looking down the shaft from two levels up, holds out a card with the word written on it. Larry points at the card and does not say it. The turntable stops. The punch lands there: Larry's finger, the card, and a spiral of stopped turntables above and below. Sibyl gives what happened after the real run: the owner ruled that Fable writes and judges comedy and nothing else, and the loop became a tool. Eppy: 'Sixteen. And a card.' The turn to the audience lands here, at the bottom of the spiral, once the loop has stopped. Larry looks straight up the shaft at the lens: 'I didn't choose that word. Somebody posted it. That's how it works. Everything on this show starts with what you post, and a puppet of you says what you published. Not an easier word. Yours. So you make the show, and I get as many goes at it as it takes. And if you tag the show, we look where you point. Looking is all I can promise.' Button, Larry: 'Point at something short.'
format: the sports desk's statistics, turning into a demonstration
notes: Answers all three parts. The descent explains where the work of making the show actually went, in the sheet's numbers; the making of the making-of is real and literal (the sheet's step 6: a tool will render every line of this script and report what it heard); and the recursion ends with a workaround, the word shown and not spoken, then with the owner's ruling as the sheet records it. Care with five things. The sheet does not say this word was among the lines rendered sixteen times, so the script must not link them: the tally is on 'a line' and the word is in the next room. Tokens are 'effective tokens' as the sheet defines them, and never money. 'Ted Walling' may be a real person's name: it appears only as text on the readout, as what was heard, and never becomes a character. Whose post the word came from is never said or shown. Whatever the readouts on the lower turntables show must be what the tool really reported for those lines, or be blank: no invented mishearings. The depth of the spiral is staging and is given no number. Each level is a smaller part of the level above that the camera flies into, then a vertical shaft of nested loops. The owner's addition lands at the bottom of the spiral, after the card has stopped the loop, and it gives the loop its reason: the words are other people's, and may be respelled but never swapped. The terms say the misheard words came from real people's posts, and that is all Larry says of it: 'somebody posted it', never who. His wording is a draft; it promises a look and nothing about what gets used.

The words get fewer but stay the sheet's facts. premise: Sibyl has the fact sheet in her hand and reads how the show is made from the top. Then the camera goes into the page, because the sheet's last sections describe the sheet being written, and what was taken out of it, and what was put back.

One passes close enough to read, and is read: 'The first kazoo looked like a submarine; I redrew it.' Larry: 'They took out the submarine?' Sibyl: 'There was no record of the submarine.' 'And now?' The structural joke: the cumulative form is the recursion, and the verses cannot help nesting.
